Title: How Do Ants Make Sense of Gravity? A Boltzmann Walker Analysis of Lasius niger Trajectories on Various Inclines
Authors: Khuong, Anaïs | Lecheval, Valentin | Fournier, Richard | Blanco, Stéphane | Weitz, Sébastian | Bezian, Jean-Jacques | Gautrais, Jacques
ColonySize: Three field colonies
SampleSize: 69 individual trajectories per inclination, 23 per colony, 345 trajectories total
ExperimentalConditions: Single worker released on unmarked 0.5 m canvas at five inclines from horizontal to pi/3. Tracking at 25 Hz after the initial 1 cm, ending at 0.2 m from the origin.
FoodCondition: Sugar water at holding bowl, no food target on canvas
MethodsSection: PDF pp. 2–3 Results, Data set and pp. 7–8 Methods, Experimental device and setup
ResultsSection: PDF pp. 3–6, Effect of inclination and extended walker analysis
SupplementaryMaterial: Dataset S1 (10.1371/journal.pone.0076531.s005) reread and recomputed. Other inclination archives and movies not independently processed.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Worker motion speed, turning and path occupancy over inclinations
OriginalMeasurement: Speed at pi/3 was about one third of flat speed. Re-extracted flat data have median per-track mean rates of 50.643 for 25 Hz path length and 38.133 for 1 s chords.
Unit: mm/s for derived flat measures
StatisticalUncertainty: Incline effect on speed Kruskal–Wallis H(4)=170.96, p<0.001. Derived flat summaries are descriptive across 69 tracks, not independent-frame confidence intervals.
ReadingScope: PDF pp. 2–3 Results, Data set and pp. 7–8 Methods, Experimental device and setup. PDF pp. 3–6, Effect of inclination and extended walker analysis. Figs. 1–5. Table 1.
Limitations: Freely walking with no experimental load. Path and chord speeds depend on sampling and tracking noise. Incline effects are not a 3D nest-route validation.

Title: The Orientation of Two Allied Species of British Ant, I. Visual Direction Finding in Acanthomyops (Lasius) niger
Authors: Carthy, J. D.
Population: British laboratory population, collection detail not used
ColonySize: Experimental groups about 100 workers
SampleSize: 12 marked workers in the white/red comparison, with repeated runs within workers
ExperimentalConditions: Trained individuals retrieved larvae from a circular arena. Rotation, altered lighting, eye varnish and dark trials changed cues.
FoodCondition: Larval retrieval task, no food choice assay
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Return-track vagrance under manipulated visual conditions
OriginalMeasurement: Seven of 12 workers had individually significant white/red differences. The pooled comparison was not significant.
Unit: workers with within-individual differences, dimensionless track vagrance
StatisticalUncertainty: The pooled null and heterogeneity across workers are reported on p. 291.
ReadingScope: pp. 276–281, Methods and training. pp. 289–296, rotation and light interventions. Figs. 12–14. Tables II–IV.
Limitations: Trained brood return is a boundary on vision-free explanations. It does not measure spontaneous food discovery or assign a turning or memory coefficient.

Title: Discovering search behaviour in black garden ant trajectories
Authors: Bonavita, Perrine | Albino, Marius | Gautrais, Jacques | Fourcassié, Vincent | Combe, Maud | Lacour, Loic | Eibner, Simon | Jost, Christian
Population: French laboratory colonies, plus the F01 Toulouse dataset
ColonySize: Three queenless colonies in new paired assay, separate from the archived trajectories
SampleSize: 69 archived horizontal tracks reanalysed. New data from 60 workers, 20 per colony, each in two light treatments.
ExperimentalConditions: Passively transferred individual releases into an unfamiliar clean arena. Starting-point-relative and camera-frame analyses. In new assay, 725 ± 24.5 lx white or 17.6 ± 0.6 lx red, paired and randomized.
FoodCondition: No food target in the filmed arena
MethodsSection: PDF pp. 3–6, Data, model, additional light experiments and statistical methods
SupplementaryMaterial: PLOS S1 File checked at Tables S1.1–S1.3. Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.19203503 cited by authors, not reanalysed.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Direction-conditioned segment length, turning and speed
OriginalMeasurement: Archived data had start-relative segment length OR 0.46 [0.37, 0.58]. White-light speed contrast away minus towards start was −2.27 [−3.03, −1.50] mm/s, red −1.70 [−2.53, −0.88] mm/s. Red-light turning and segment-length contrasts were not significant.
Unit: odds ratio as reported by authors and mm/s
StatisticalUncertainty: 95% model intervals as reported. White-light segment-length contrast p=0.042 did not meet the corrected 0.006 threshold.
ReadingScope: PDF pp. 3–6, Data, model, additional light experiments and statistical methods. PDF pp. 6–10, Results. Figs. 1–4 and S1.1–S1.12. Tables S1.1–S1.3.
Limitations: The archived analysis reuses F01 and is not an independent data set. New light trials are independent data, but passive release around an origin does not isolate a home-vector mechanism. Fig. 4 simulations are not measurements.
EvidenceRelation: Primary experiment with a separately identified reanalysis of F01

Title: Sensitivity and feeding efficiency of the black garden ant Lasius niger to sugar resources
Authors: Detrain, Claire | Prieur, Jacques
ColonySize: Four source colonies of about 1000 ants
SampleSize: Intake assay 6 groups of 5 scouts per sucrose concentration, drawn from 3 colonies. Acceptance assay 7 replicates of groups of 15 per concentration per sugar.
ExperimentalConditions: Antennal contact without mandible immersion and actual drinking were scored separately after feeder access. Feeding acceptance is feeding events divided by all contacts.
FoodCondition: Three days of deprivation with water. Water control and five sugars at 0.001–2.5 M where soluble.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Contact-conditioned feeding acceptance and intake
OriginalMeasurement: Fitted acceptance onset was 0.014 M melezitose, 0.030 M sucrose, 0.078 M glucose and 0.083 M fructose. Trehalose did not show the comparable increasing response. 1 M sucrose drinking spans less than 10 s to over 3 min.
Unit: mol/L and seconds
StatisticalUncertainty: Threshold is fitted relative to the upper water-control 95% limit. Fig. 3 shows mean ± SD across replicate groups. Intake varied by concentration, Kruskal–Wallis statistic 29.98, p<0.001.
Limitations: The paper does not estimate a distance at which hidden food is first detected. The fitting parameters describe post-contact acceptance and not feeder discovery or bulk pickup.

Title: Food transport in ants: Do Lasius niger foragers maximize their individual load?
Authors: Mailleux, Anne-Catherine | Deneubourg, Jean-Louis | Detrain, Claire
ColonySize: Four queenless colonies, 1000–2000 workers
SampleSize: 63 single-tested scouts that found both drops, from 4 colonies
ExperimentalConditions: First drop in 6 × 6 cm arena. Second drop was installed 9 cm away after first contact and was accessible on the way back.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived, two 0.7 µL drops of 0.6 M sucrose
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Ingested volume, drinking duration and trail marking after partial feeding
OriginalMeasurement: Mean first intake 0.47 ± 0.25 µL, second intake 0.28 ± 0.20 µL, total 0.75 ± 0.30 µL. First drinking time 51 ± 12 s. 38% marked the first return segment, 84% marked by the second segment.
Unit: µL of solution, seconds and percent of scouts
StatisticalUncertainty: Mean ± SD, N=63. Time between drops was 58 ± 33 s for first-segment trailers and 134 ± 87 s for non-trailers, Mann–Whitney p<0.0001.
Limitations: Only workers finding both drops were analyzed. The second drop on the return leg constrains loaded-return policy. Liquid in crop is not external cargo or maximum carrying mass.

Title: Decision making in ant foragers (Lasius niger) facing conflicting private and social information
Authors: Grüter, Christoph | Czaczkes, Tomer J. | Ratnieks, Francis L. W.
ColonySize: Eight queenless colonies, 700–1000 workers
SampleSize: 6 colonies in the learning experiment, 8 in the trail-strength assay. For Fig. 2b 333 naive ants tested individually, colony random effects.
ExperimentalConditions: T-junction with fresh branch paper to isolate memory. Separate paper marked by 1, 5 or 20 passages, followed by conflicting memory/trail treatments.
FoodCondition: 1.8 M sucrose in training, experimental branch choice at a marked decision line
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Binary branch choice by naive and experienced foragers and time to commit
OriginalMeasurement: Correct memory-only choices were 74.6% after one visit and 95.3% after three. Naive marked-branch choices were 61.6% with one passage and 70.2% with 20. After one visit with a conflicting trail, 84.4% chose the previously rewarded branch.
Unit: percent of individual branch choices, passages as nominal trail treatment
StatisticalUncertainty: Learning contrast 0 vs 1 visit p=0.002, 1 vs 3 p=0.014. One vs 20 passage increase p=0.107. Conflicting trail-strength effect p=0.69.
ReadingScope: pp. 142–144, Methods, experiments 1–5. pp. 144–146, Results, experiments 1–5. Figs. 1–4.
Limitations: Choice accuracy is conditional on maze, recent visits and food. A learned preference still makes errors and supplies neither a fixed expiry nor a general priority law.

Title: Ant foraging on complex trails: route learning and the role of trail pheromones in Lasius niger
Authors: Czaczkes, Tomer J. | Grüter, Christoph | Ellis, Laura | Wood, Elizabeth | Ratnieks, Francis L. W.
ColonySize: Eight queenless colonies, 500–1500 workers with some brood
SampleSize: Repeated choices within individual foragers across up to seven visits. Fig. 3b N=186, 164 and 124 choices as plotted. Fig. 4 Appendix identifies same-ant repeated observations.
ExperimentalConditions: Double T maze, short or doubled-length paths. Repeating and alternating routes. Paper overlays removed after every visit, at final visit only or retained.
FoodCondition: Four days of deprivation, 1 M sucrose at the assigned endpoint
SupplementaryMaterial: Appendix A1/A2 in article read. Separate online media not used.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Route accuracy, learning with or without trail and error-dependent marking
OriginalMeasurement: Without maintained trails, 97% correct choices at repeating versus 68% at alternating bifurcations over visits. On alternating paths 56% versus 73% correct choices without versus with retained trail. On the unmarked final trip, prior trail exposure was associated with 73% versus 62% accuracy.
Unit: percent of bifurcation choices
StatisticalUncertainty: Retained-versus-removed contrast z=6.756, p<0.00001. Unmarked final comparison z=−2.322, p=0.0326.
ReadingScope: pp. 189–190, Materials and methods, experiments 1–3. pp. 190–193, Results. Figs. 1–4 and 6. Appendix Tables A1–A2 pp. 195–196.
Limitations: Trial-history effect and immediate cue use are different endpoints. This learning effect is assay-specific and was not recovered in B2-P03.

Title: How food type and brood influence foraging decisions of Lasius niger scouts
Authors: Portha, Stéphane | Deneubourg, Jean-Louis | Detrain, Claire
ColonySize: Four mother colonies of 1500–2000 workers in the Methods origin description, split into queenless brood and broodless nests
SampleSize: Table 1 has 31 sucrose/brood, 28 sucrose/no brood, 58 protein/brood and 41 protein/no brood scouts. The Methods separately describe five trial nests per brood condition.
ExperimentalConditions: Single scout per trial on a fresh 22 cm bridge to a 6 × 6 cm arena. Video distinguishes exploration, return with and without marking, and liquid ingestion.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived, alternating 3 µL drops of 1 M sucrose or filtered maggot preparation
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Food-type and brood effects on post-contact drinking, return and marking frequency
OriginalMeasurement: Among returning scouts, 84% from brood-containing nests versus 65% from broodless nests marked after sucrose. After protein those percentages were 61% and 35%. Among all observed scouts, exploration was 6% and 10% after sucrose versus 43% and 45% after protein.
Unit: percent of scouts in the stated subset, seconds and µL in Table 1
StatisticalUncertainty: Returning-ants mark/no-mark distribution across four treatments chi-square=13.757, p=0.003. Mark intensity among trailers did not show the same treatment effect.
ReadingScope: pp. 116–117, Methods. pp. 117–121, Results and interpretation. Figs. 1–4. Table 1.
Limitations: Some arrivals and bridge falls were excluded. A change in probability of marking is not a change in chemical mass per mark. This single-source assay does not compare equal-distance feeder choice.

Title: Does substrate coarseness matter for foraging ants? An experiment with Lasius niger (Hymenoptera; Formicidae)
Authors: Bernadou, Abel | Fourcassié, Vincent
Population: University Paul Sabatier campus, Toulouse, France
ColonySize: Five stock colonies, standardized groups about 500 workers each
SampleSize: Locomotion 25 workers per texture, 5 per group. Separate choice and conditioning experiments.
ExperimentalConditions: 120 s worker path tests without food on fine 400–560 µm or coarse 1250–1400 µm calcareous sand. Other assays tested spontaneous choice and rewarded tactile learning.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived, sucrose in familiarization, no food in recorded movement test
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Distance travelled per time, turning, sand choice and conditioning
OriginalMeasurement: Linear speed 2.63 ± 0.20 cm/s fine and 2.21 ± 0.17 cm/s coarse. Directionality 0.67 ± 0.03 versus 0.71 ± 0.02. Mean free path contrast was not significant and naive ants showed no texture preference in the tested choices.
Unit: cm/s and dimensionless directionality
StatisticalUncertainty: Paper reports means ± 95% CI half-width. Speed F(1,40)=16.53, p<0.001. Mean free path p=0.077.
Limitations: Tracked movement averages are neither maxima nor cargo-specific speeds. Terrain effect cannot be fitted by the single shared maximum without a matched motor assay.

Title: Collective exploration and area marking in the ant Lasius niger
Authors: Devigne, Cédric | Detrain, Claire
ColonySize: Ten source colonies with 500–1000 individuals, nine in exploration
SampleSize: 13 early branch-count trials, 7 complete flow series and 11 late branch-selection trials. Separate marked-paper encounter assays.
ExperimentalConditions: No-food new areas on symmetric 30 cm branches at 30 degrees with landmarks screened. Separate explored paper from own colony, another colony and unmarked controls.
FoodCondition: Exploration after 3 days of deprivation, no reward on the branches
MethodsSection: p. 358, Materials and methods, collective exploration and area marking
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Outgoing flow, branch bias and response to exploratory marking
OriginalMeasurement: Significant branch imbalance in 7/13 early and 2/11 late trials. Mean flow 107.5 ± 110.4 per 15 min at one hour versus 37.13 ± 37.5 at 20 h. The winning branch exceeded 70% in only 16% of early trials.
Unit: ants per 15 min, fraction of trial-level branch biases
StatisticalUncertainty: Mean ± SD. Per-trial binomial threshold p<0.05. Marked-area occupancy did not significantly differ across the tested conditions.
ReadingScope: p. 358, Materials and methods, collective exploration and area marking. pp. 358–361, Results and discussion. Figs. 1–3. Tables 1–3.
Limitations: Food-free exploratory marking is distinct from food-trail pheromone. Paper assays did not isolate the compounds or an individual revisit penalty.

Title: Effect of Trail Bifurcation Asymmetry and Pheromone Presence or Absence on Trail Choice by Lasius niger Ants
Authors: Forster, Antonia | Czaczkes, Tomer J. | Warner, Emma | Woodall, Tom | Martin, Emily | Ratnieks, Francis L. W.
ColonySize: Four queenless 500–1000-worker source colonies split into trail-laying and test fragments
SampleSize: 570 naive first decisions in experiment 2, nested within the four source colonies. Groups of ten per configuration.
ExperimentalConditions: Mirrored 90-degree Y-maze with variable branch asymmetry. Paper had 15 observed deposits per 3 cm. Equal marking on both arms or one marked arm.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived. 1 M sucrose used to produce trails and stimulate test groups before naive branch choices.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Naive choice at a specified decision line
OriginalMeasurement: With equally marked arms, 47% went right at 45:45 degrees and 73% chose the straight arm at 0:90 degrees. With one marked arm, 336/570 chose it across conditions.
Unit: percent or count of individual choices
StatisticalUncertainty: Equal-marking asymmetry effect z=6.971, p<0.00001. Pooled marked-arm preference p<0.0001. In experiment 2 the graded angle effect alone was not significant, p=0.473.
ReadingScope: pp. 769–772, Materials and Methods, experiments 1–2. pp. 772–774, Results and discussion. Figs. 1–3.
Limitations: Geometry and cue placement both matter. Mark counts do not determine mass and physical maze constraints do not isolate a cardinal-grid weight.

Title: Synergy between social and private information increases foraging efficiency in ants
Authors: Czaczkes, Tomer J. | Grüter, Christoph | Jones, Sam M. | Ratnieks, Francis L. W.
ColonySize: Donor and test colony fragments
SampleSize: Repeated trajectory segments within individually observed workers. Independent group counts require the methods supplement.
ExperimentalConditions: 21 cm straight paper walkway. A fresh central 7 cm strip interrupted the marked trail. Experienced or naive ants, one or 20 donor passages, home-range-mark controls.
FoodCondition: Sucrose feeder, training and tests with one or three prior return visits for experienced ants
SupplementaryMaterial: Main text references S1 and S2. The main paper and its figures were reread. Supplement not independently recovered.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Path speed, sinuosity, U-turn rate and marking when leaving a marked section
OriginalMeasurement: Experienced ants were 30% faster and 30% straighter on marked than unmarked walkway. Exiting the marked section increased U-turning with or without previous visits.
Unit: relative percent change and worker U-turn frequency
StatisticalUncertainty: Speed contrasts p<0.001 and sinuosity contrasts p<0.003. U-turn contrast z>2.78, p<0.01. No significant dose effect on the listed endpoints for one versus 20 donor passages.
Limitations: A local directional correction is supported at this abrupt cue gap. There is no unique predecessor or direction-to-food vector in the result. Speed change is conditional on memory.

Title: The Effect of Trail Pheromone and Path Confinement on Learning of Complex Routes in the Ant Lasius niger
Authors: Czaczkes, Tomer J. | Weichselgartner, Tobias | Bernadou, Abel | Heinze, Jürgen
ColonySize: Eight queenless colonies, about 1000 workers and brood
SampleSize: Two route sides per treatment per colony. The cleaned workbook contains 4930 rows for 260 ant labels within eight colony labels, with repeated fork/trip observations and missing choices.
ExperimentalConditions: Alternating double-bifurcation maze, open or physically constrained training. Trail retained or removed. All tests use open, unmarked final maze.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived with water, 1 M sucrose at the assigned endpoint
MethodsSection: Methods, Study species, Experimental design and Statistical analysis
ResultsSection: Results, Decision making and Pheromone deposition
SupplementaryMaterial: S1 File and S1 Table were opened. Limited descriptive workbook checks, no refit of the authors’ GLMM.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Final unmarked route accuracy after training with or without pheromone
OriginalMeasurement: Prior trail did not improve final unmarked accuracy. Confinement was associated with more errors at the first choice.
Unit: individual binary route choices within worker and colony
StatisticalUncertainty: Final test GLMM z=−0.46, p=0.65 for pheromone. First-choice confinement z=−3.3, p=0.0017. Multiple comparisons were corrected in the article.
ReadingScope: Methods, Study species, Experimental design and Statistical analysis. Results, Decision making and Pheromone deposition. Figs. 1–3. S1 Table.
Limitations: The null concerns learning carried into a later unmarked trial. It does not rule out immediate cue use. Different colonies and manipulations from F07.

Title: Pheromone trail following is not modulated by previous visit to food location, distance travelled, or travel direction in the ant Lasius niger
Authors: Poissonnier, Laure-Anne | Winter, D. | Olivera-Rodriguez, F.-J. | Werneke, C. | Czaczkes, Tomer J.
ColonySize: Queenless 500–1500-worker colonies
SampleSize: Exp. 1 workbook contains 102 individual tracks in four groups of 25 or 26, from 6 colonies. Exp. 2 has 398 choices from 8 colonies, groups of 99 or 100.
ExperimentalConditions: A4 arena after 20 or 100 cm walkway, 1 cm central strip either side of the trail. Separate mirrored 120-degree Y-maze tests travel direction and previous feeder experience.
FoodCondition: Three or four days deprived. Solvent controls, hindgut extract 4 glands/mL DCM. Separate feeder training in Exp. 2.
SupplementaryMaterial: Springer ESM Rmd and XLSX inspected. Fig. 2 counts and Fig. 5 choice totals recomputed without rerunning authors’ mixed models.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Open-arena strip occupancy and initial Y-maze choice, analysed separately
OriginalMeasurement: Workbook trail vs solvent mean occupancy fractions are 0.53892 vs 0.23722 after a short approach and 0.47134 vs 0.23179 after a long approach. 348/398 Y choices on the marked arm.
Unit: proportion of frames per ant and counts of first choices
StatisticalUncertainty: Arena reported marking estimate 0.1964, p<0.01 on the fitted scale. Approach length and interaction p=0.76 and 0.77 for occupancy. No significant speed benefit. Y direction/experience tests all p>0.54.
ReadingScope: PDF pp. 2–4, Methods and Experiments 1–2. PDF pp. 4–6, Results. Figs. 1–5.
Limitations: Printed Methods n=26 each is nominal. Fig. 2 and workbook resolve unequal analyzed counts. An occupancy effect does not estimate detection distance, direction of travel, continuous trail-following fidelity or recruitment.

Title: Negative feedback in ants: crowding results in less trail pheromone deposition
Authors: Czaczkes, Tomer J. | Grüter, Christoph | Ratnieks, Francis L. W.
Journal: Journal of the Royal Society Interface 10 20121009
ColonySize: Queenless 500–1000 workers with some brood
SampleSize: Five colonies for trail-width manipulations. Ten colonies and repeated individual journeys for the bead test, generally 40–44 workers per condition in Fig. 3.
ExperimentalConditions: 20 cm paper trail at widths of 5 or 20 mm, low or high traffic. Separate plain, colony-hydrocarbon coated and no-bead treatments.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived with water, 1 M sucrose for trail work
SupplementaryMaterial: S2/S3 cited in main article. Main text and figures used, supplemental data not independently checked.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Probability of making a mark and number of marks conditional on depositing
OriginalMeasurement: Extreme traffic conditions differed 5.6-fold in depositing fraction. In the black coated-bead versus no-bead comparison the reported depositing fractions were 0.51 vs 0.83, with 3.4 vs 9.3 marks per depositing ant.
Unit: fraction of foragers and count of deposition behaviours
StatisticalUncertainty: Crowding and trail width interacted. Narrow vs wide individual marking p=0.00017 in focal experiment. Fig. 3 shows 95% intervals.
Limitations: A reduction in marking acts is evidence of feedback. It does not give a mass decrement per collision or calibrate a saturation cap.

Title: Ants (Lasius niger) deposit more pheromone close to food sources and further from the nest but do not attempt to update erroneous pheromone trails
Authors: Czaczkes, Tomer J. | Olivera-Rodriguez, Federico-Javier | Poissonnier, Laure-Anne
ColonySize: Eight queenless wild-colony fragments, 500–2000 workers, some worker-derived male brood
SampleSize: S2 has 486 trials with a numeric total mark count, 241 previously marked and 245 unmarked. S3 has 1243 numeric segment observations nested in ants and colonies. A subset of 37 trials checked eye/video agreement.
ExperimentalConditions: Four marked/unmarked Y-maze and first-arm outcomes. Separate near-far runway assay records deposition by 10 cm segment.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived. 0.8 M sucrose in the maze, extract or DCM control.
SupplementaryMaterial: S1 model output and S2/S3 workbooks inspected. Descriptive S2 counts and means rechecked. S1 names the runway assay Experiment 3 while the main article calls it Experiment 2.
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Spatial return marking count and response to an incorrect trail
OriginalMeasurement: Mean marks 6.90 on previously marked versus 7.44 on unmarked Y-maze. Initial choice of unrewarded arm did not significantly increase marks. Marking varied along 10 cm sections and with runway length.
Unit: observed marking acts per trip or segment
StatisticalUncertainty: Marked contrast p=0.045. Wrong first arm p=0.074 and interaction p=0.289. Distance and runway length effects p<0.0001.
ReadingScope: pp. 369–371, Methods, Experiments 1–2. pp. 371–373, Results. Figs. 1–3. Table 1.
Limitations: Existing trail, feeder distance and an error manipulation test different feedback signals. No measured mass field or evidence for automatic correction of an outdated branch.

Title: Combined use of pheromone trails and visual landmarks by the common garden ant Lasius niger
Authors: Evison, Sophie E. F. | Petchey, Owen L. | Beckerman, Andrew P. | Ratnieks, Francis L. W.
ColonySize: Nine queenless soil-nest colonies, about 500–1000 workers
SampleSize: Longevity assay 5 colonies, one trial each. Traffic-level assay 9 colonies. Individual choices pooled per 20 min within each colony.
ExperimentalConditions: Stored paper trail sections, 15 cm readout, 30/125/500 establishing passages. Age series 0 to 1440 min. No-mark paper and same/different rooms as controls.
FoodCondition: Four days without diluted honey, 1 M sucrose feeder for trails
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Completing a marked paper length and loss of excess following with time
OriginalMeasurement: 500-passage trail completion dropped from about 77% to 28% at 24 h, against 30.8% control. Fitted crossing of the control took 1200–1440 min. Initial same-room advantage about 20 percentage points, about 10 after 2 h.
Unit: proportion completing 15 cm and minutes after trail establishment
StatisticalUncertainty: Age contrast t=13.4, p<0.0001. Trail age × room t=3.62, p<0.0001. Age × traffic contrasts not significant at 0.05.
ReadingScope: pp. 262–264, Materials and methods, Experiments 1–3. pp. 264–266, Results and discussion. Figs. 1–5.
Limitations: This response includes assay and cue context, possible re-establishment and visual memory. Returning to behavioral baseline is not a molecular half-life or a deposition concentration.

Title: Trail laying behaviour during food recruitment in the ant Lasius niger (L.)
Authors: Beckers, Ralph | Deneubourg, Jean-Louis | Goss, Simon
ColonySize: Eight adult colonies of 2000–3000 individuals available. Five foundation colonies less than a year old with 12–23 individuals.
SampleSize: Overall 3 adult and 5 foundation colonies. Individually marked sets of 37 recruiters across 6 adult colonies and 37 recruits across 5 adult colonies. Passage counts repeat individuals.
ExperimentalConditions: Lateral video over 20 cm cardboard bridge. Gaster-dots scored by direction and trip. Exchanged distal paper to test effect of removing prior marking.
FoodCondition: Four days deprived, 1 M sucrose in a connected arena
MethodsSection: pp. 60–62, Materials and methods, overall and individual series
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Marking frequency and intensity by trip, travel direction and colony context
OriginalMeasurement: Observed marks in both travel directions after feeder experience. Marking usually more frequent on the return and varied across workers and trips. Mean 4–6 marks per marking passage on trips two through four.
Unit: marks per marking passage or frequency per passage
StatisticalUncertainty: Figures separate colony replicates and behavioural groups. The 1000 s lifetime in Fig. 2 caption belongs to their model, not a chemical measurement.
ReadingScope: pp. 60–62, Materials and methods, overall and individual series. pp. 62–68, Results. Figs. 1–5. Tables 1–2.
Limitations: The paper scores marking acts. A depot-return path, a gland dose and a chemical half-life are separate endpoints. Initial outward scouts and experienced outbound foragers differ.

Title: Recruitment in starved nests: the role of direct and indirect interactions between scouts and nestmates in the ant Lasius niger
Authors: Mailleux, Anne-Catherine | Buffin, Aurélie | Detrain, Claire | Deneubourg, Jean-Louis
ColonySize: Three mature queenless colonies, 800–1400 workers, no brood
SampleSize: 28, 25 and 26 single-scout assays at one, four and eight days deprived. Nestmates observed within each 20 min scout window.
ExperimentalConditions: Nest video identifies antennal/trophallactic contact, no contact, exit and deposition near entrance. First feeding scout and food apparatus removed after initial return and exit.
FoodCondition: 1, 4 and 8 days of deprivation, 3 µL of 0.6 M sucrose
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Departure by deprivation and contact category, relay marks before feeder exposure
OriginalMeasurement: Non-contact group departure rose from 0.38 to 0.72. 25% of 24 and 32% of 25 departing food recipients at four/eight days marked without ever visiting the food source. No such relay at one day.
Unit: fraction of classified nestmates and time to exit
StatisticalUncertainty: Non-contact departure chi-square=9.39, p<0.01. Four/eight-day relay contrast not significant. Scout marking fraction did not significantly change with deprivation, p=0.33.
ReadingScope: pp. 560–562, Materials and methods. pp. 562–566, Results and discussion. Fig. 1. Tables 1–3.
Limitations: Departure is an observed result. Scout chemical triggering is an inference, with no isolated dose or threshold. No evidence of contact encoding target coordinates.

Title: 3,4-Dihydroisocoumarins, a New Class of Ant Trail Pheromones
Authors: Bestmann, Hans Jürgen | Kern, Friedrich | Schäfer, Doris | Witschel, Matthias Christian
Journal: Angewandte Chemie International Edition in English 31 795–796
ActualExperimentalSpecies: Lasius niger focal. Formica rufa, F. fusca and F. sanguinea separately analysed in the paper.
Population: Laboratory material identified by Hasenfuss, geographic worker provenance not specified for the focal tests
ColonySize: Focal lab colony mentioned, worker counts for behavioral test not reported
SampleSize: 40 L. niger rectal sacs pooled for Fig. 1. Behavioral and electroantennogram replication counts not reported in the short communication.
ExperimentalConditions: GC–MS comparison to synthetic compounds, enantiomer trails, electroantennogram and behavioral tests. Formica responses are separate.
FoodCondition: Synthetic trail test, no diet treatment used for this audit
MethodsSection: pp. 795–796, synthesis, solid-phase GC–MS and trail biotest description
ActualMeasuredEndpoint: Identification and behavioral activity of a L. niger hindgut trail component
OriginalMeasurement: (R)-3,4-dihydro-8-hydroxy-3,5,7-trimethylisocoumarin assigned to the natural compound. Compound 5 elicited following at 500 pg per artificial trail. (R) was preferred to (S) in the tested choice.
Unit: pg/trail for applied synthetic test dose
StatisticalUncertainty: No dose-response interval, matched assay threshold or uncertainty estimate for dose. EAG activity and trail following are separately scored.
ReadingScope: pp. 795–796, synthesis, solid-phase GC–MS and trail biotest description. p. 796, species-specific and stereochemical tests. Scheme 1 and Fig. 1. Tables 1–2.
Limitations: Test dose is not mass per natural mark, a detection cutoff, a diffusion coefficient, a duration or proof that all components are known. Formica results were not transferred.

Title: Collective decision making in a heterogeneous environment: Lasius niger colonies preferentially forage at easy to learn locations
Authors: Grüter, Christoph | Maitre, Diane | Blakey, Alex | Cole, Rosemary | Ratnieks, Francis L. W.
Population: University of Lausanne campus, Switzerland, focal experiment 1
ColonySize: Six queenless colony fragments about 1000 workers with some brood in experiment 1. Separate colony sample in experiment 2.
SampleSize: Experiment 1 two mirrored trials per colony and 103 first naive choices recorded. Experiment 2 collective landmark arm tested 10 colonies.
